extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in moral/philosophical reflections on love, courtship, and manners (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and observations about manners, modesty, courtship, and sexual conduct — especially moderation, coyness, honesty, and protection of reputation in amorous affairs. The text mixes moral prescription with examples and literary quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty in public eating
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not display appetite at a public table; appearing to eat eagerly takes away from a lady's grace and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people who are unwilling to appear at table with an appetite; a man who cannot endure to see another eat; Turkish men who never suffer themselves to be seen making their repast. Implication: restraint and modesty in eating preserve decorum and attractiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject self-denaturing fanaticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid extreme self-contempt or self-denaturing practices (fasting, mutilation, forced solitude) done to 'honour' nature by disnaturing oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticises sects/peoples who cut and mangle themselves, who never speak, who curse birth and bless death. He calls such conduct monstrous and warns intellect misapplied becomes dangerous. Anti-pattern: ascetic acts that increase misfortune rather than virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not invent unnecessary miseries
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not increase the inevitable inconveniences of life by voluntarily inventing additional hardships or imaginary deformities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted admonition: 'thou hast enough inconveniences that are inevitable, without increasing them by thy own invention.' Practical guidance: prioritise natural, essential duties over self-imposed, particular, and fantastic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware false modesty that teases or invites
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty that half-reveals or is performed to prompt curiosity is treacherous; hiding only to show can excite imagination more than frankness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ladies covering necks with network, painters shadowing pictures; Martial and Ovid quotations illustrate that half-openness can 'glut and disgust' or 'draw us on to guess at more than is meant.' Anti-pattern: ostentatious or performative modesty intended to provoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value delay, gradation, and coyness in courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: A respectful, timorous, coy, and secret love (gradual advances, preambles, glances, bows, words) is more pleasing than impetuosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises Spanish and Italian restraint and suggests teaching ladies to 'spin out their favours' so that desire and reward are extended. Practical effect: prolonging pursuit increases esteem, pleasure, and the duration of attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the chase/process over mere fruition
rubrics_metrics.description: One who seeks only the act of fruition and not the stages of courtship is unfit; the value lies in the pursuit and its gradations, not only the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation: 'He who has no fruition but in fruition... ought not to introduce himself in our school.' Analogy: palace approached by long galleries—more steps increase honour of the uppermost seat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve reserve; avoid complete surrender
rubrics_metrics.description: Total surrender of a woman's person (or one partner completely surrendering) is hazardous; keeping reserve preserves honor and desirability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: 'when they wholly surrender themselves up to the mercy of our fidelity and constancy they run a mighty hazard.' Encourage graduated concession rather than instantaneous abandonment of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Win the will, not merely the body
rubrics_metrics.description: The true object of courtship is to gain the will and affection, not only the bodily act; the woman's will is what should be served and won.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported Italian justification that 'women sell nothing but their bodies; the will is too free and too much of its own to be exposed to sale.' Montaigne: 'tis the will they undertake and they have reason.' Practical: aim for consented affection rather than transactional intercourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require consent and desire for genuine love
rubrics_metrics.description: Loving a body without its consent or desire is not true affection; consent distinguishes genuine love from mere possession of a body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative (and condemned) examples: desecration of statues, violation of corpses, Periander's post-mortem conjugal enjoyment. Moral: consent and reciprocal feeling are necessary components of legitimate affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether affection is genuine or instrumental
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether a person's company pleases you for its own sake or only for instrumental reasons (status, convenience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people who 'had rather lend that than their coach' — imparting only physically; check degree of favour and esteem versus mere usage. Practical: look for signs of genuine attachment rather than utilitarian motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust partial or half-given favors
rubrics_metrics.description: When favours are given incompletely or by halves, treachery or insincerity may be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation: 'they sometimes go to't by halves' (Martial). Guidance: partial compliance can conceal lack of real affection; assess whole behaviour, not isolated acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise eagerness; forbid facility/promptness in granting favors
rubrics_metrics.description: Facility and promptness in love are signs of eagerness and should be avoided; measured, orderly granting of favors is more alluring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to Plato who 'declares that, in all sorts of love, facility and promptness are forbidden to the defendant.' Practical tip: conceal eagerness, prolong the approach, and use modesty strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physically examine fitness before marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Before marriage, evaluate the physical capacity and fitness of partners to ensure marital duties can be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's suggested law: judges should see young men stripped and women to the girdle to determine fitness. Intention: practical pre-marriage assessment to avoid disappointment and deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weakness or insufficiency may justify marital separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical weakness or insufficiency lawfully breaks a marriage; inability to satisfy can be legitimate grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation: 'weakness and insufficiency lawfully break a marriage.' The standard: competence in marital functions is a valid concern when assessing marital suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not feign youth or prowess where you wish to please
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impudent to present your imperfections and imbecilities as virtues; do not pretend vigor or abilities you lack in order to please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises against strutting with 'one poor inch of pitiful vigour' and mocks the elderly who pretend great virility. Practical: match conduct to real capacity; avoid ridiculous displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in pleasures; philosophy recommends moderation, not total abstinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy does not condemn natural pleasures outright but preaches moderation and warns against allowing the mind to inflame bodily appetites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: 'The appetites of the body ought not to be augmented by the mind.' On the other hand, in aged or weakened bodies, moderate indulgence can be excused to restore cheerfulness. Balance is the criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use love moderately as a restorative in old age
rubrics_metrics.description: For those without other vocation or suffering age-related decline, love (moderately practised) can restore vigilance, sobriety, grace, and cheerfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recommends love as a physician-like prescription for older men to rouse body and spirit, but emphasises moderation and avoiding dotage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind and body pleasures should be balanced
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither mind nor body should domineer to the other's prejudice; the mind should not needlessly stir bodily appetites, nor should it be made a slave to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: it's unjust to treat pleasures as purely corporeal or spiritual; both should co-operate. Practical: cultivate pleasures that are sweet and useful to both faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relationships maintained by pity or charity
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not accept or cultivate affectionate relations that arise only from the other's pity; dependence upon charity is degrading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'If they can only be kind to us out of pity, I had much rather die than live upon charity.' Standard: desire reciprocity and genuine regard, not merciful condescension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep promises and avoid ingratitude, treachery, malice, cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: In amorous commerce, maintain integrity: be faithful, avoid breaking with hatred, and do not practice ingratitude or cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts his own conduct: spared promises, was 'better than my word,' faithful even amid inconstancy. Practical ethical standard: honesty and benevolence in private affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect a woman's reputation; assume hazard to acquit her
rubrics_metrics.description: When arranging assignations or meetings, act to shield the woman's honour and reputation; contrive meetings in ways that are less suspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne says he always 'wholly taken upon myself alone the hazard of our assignations' and contrived unusual meetings as less suspected. Standard: the man should protect the woman's social standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in upbringing and discipline of women and servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme strictness in upbringing often produces no better outcomes than greater liberty; there should be moderation and much left to discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: 'ladies who have been strict with their maids have had no better luck than those who allowed them greater liberty.' Recommendation: avoid excessive discipline; trust reasonable discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge yourself honestly as you judge others
rubrics_metrics.description: Be an impartial judge of actions, confess the truth when it is against you as readily as when it favours you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne acknowledges mutual unjust judging between sexes and emphasizes self-awareness: 'I confess the truth when it makes against me.' Practical advice: apply same standards inwardly as outwardly.
